GHSA-3r6v-f3jh-vvqm.description: The validating recursor's NSEC handler does not distinguish parent-side delegation NSEC records from authoritative child-side NSECs. When a parent zone returns NXDOMAIN with the signed NSEC at the zone cut the implementation accepts that record as covering both the queried name and the synthesized wildcard, and returns `Proof::Secure`. The resolver then serves NXDOMAIN with AD=1 for names that legitimately exist in the child zone, contrary to RFC 6840 §4.1, which requires that an ancestor-delegation NSEC authenticate only the absence of DS at the cut owner and never the nonexistence of names below it. The forged response uses only records that are genuinely signed and publicly retrievable from the parent, so no key compromise is required; an attacker only needs to deliver one such response (on-path, via a rogue parent nameserver, or by winning a port+TXID race). Because the recursor caches the resulting negative under the (child., NS) key during its delegation walk, every subsequent client query for any name strictly below the cut short-circuits to the cached denial for up to the negative TTL. A similar issue affects validation of wildcard nonexistence proofs in NOERROR responses. There is another variant related to names with DNAME records, which are also mentioned in RFC 6840 §4.1. #### Reporter Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.title: Hickory DNS's Record Cache Accepts AUTHORITY-Section NS from Sibling Zone via Parent-Pool Zone-Context Elevation
GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.description:
# Summary

The Hickory DNS project's experimental `hickory-recursor` crate's record cache (`DnsLru`) stores records from DNS responses keyed by each record's own (name, type), not by the query that triggered the response. `cache_response()` in `crates/recursor/src/lib.rs` chains `ANSWER`, `AUTHORITY`, and `ADDITIONAL` sections into one record iterator before insertion. The bailiwick filter it applies uses the zone context of the NS pool that serviced the lookup, not the zone being queried.

This creates a cross-zone poisoning path. When Hickory builds the NS pool for `attacker.poc.` it uses the parent `poc.` `NS` pool (`ns.zone() = "poc."`). If the `poc.` nameserver under the attacker's control includes in its response's `AUTHORITY` section a record for a sibling zone like `victim.poc. NS ns.evil.poc.`, the bailiwick check `is_subzone("poc.", "victim.poc.")` passes (`victim.poc.` is a subdomain of `poc.`). The record is stored under `(victim.poc., NS)` in the shared cache.

Subsequently, any client querying a name in `victim.poc`. causes Hickory to build its NS pool from the poisoned cache entry, routing queries to the attacker's nameserver (`ns.evil.poc.`) rather than to the legitimate nameserver for `victim.poc.`. The legitimate `NS` for that zone receives zero queries.

This issue is fixed in `hickory-resolver` 0.26.0 with the `recursor` feature through an architectural change to response-level caching: responses are stored keyed by the originating query `(name, type)`. A response to `(attacker.poc. NS)` is stored only under that key and cannot affect the `(victim.poc., NS)` cache entry.

Hickory DNS believes this issue has been present in all published versions of the experimental `hickory-recursor` crate, which has now been folded into the `hickory-resolver` crate under the non-default `recursor` feature flag. The `hickory-recursor` crate will not receive any updates going forward and all users should migrate to `hickory-resolver` with the `recursor` feature.

Users of the `hickory-dns` binary configured with the opt-in `recursor` feature and a configuration acting as a recursive resolver should update to 0.26.0+.

GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.description:
# Summary

The Hickory DNS project's experimental `hickory-recursor` crate's record cache (`DnsLru`) stores records from DNS responses keyed by each record's own (name, type), not by the query that triggered the response. `cache_response()` in `crates/recursor/src/lib.rs` chains `ANSWER`, `AUTHORITY`, and `ADDITIONAL` sections into one record iterator before insertion. The bailiwick filter it applies uses the zone context of the NS pool that serviced the lookup, not the zone being queried.

This creates a cross-zone poisoning path. When Hickory builds the NS pool for `attacker.poc.` it uses the parent `poc.` `NS` pool (`ns.zone() = "poc."`). If the `poc.` nameserver under the attacker's control includes in its response's `AUTHORITY` section a record for a sibling zone like `victim.poc. NS ns.evil.poc.`, the bailiwick check `is_subzone("poc.", "victim.poc.")` passes (`victim.poc.` is a subdomain of `poc.`). The record is stored under `(victim.poc., NS)` in the shared cache.

Subsequently, any client querying a name in `victim.poc`. causes Hickory to build its NS pool from the poisoned cache entry, routing queries to the attacker's nameserver (`ns.evil.poc.`) rather than to the legitimate nameserver for `victim.poc.`. The legitimate `NS` for that zone receives zero queries.

This issue is fixed in `hickory-resolver` 0.26.0 with the `recursor` feature through an architectural change to response-level caching: responses are stored keyed by the originating query `(name, type)`. A response to `(attacker.poc. NS)` is stored only under that key and cannot affect the `(victim.poc., NS)` cache entry.

Hickory DNS believes this issue has been present in all published versions of the experimental `hickory-recursor` crate, which has now been folded into the `hickory-resolver` crate under the non-default `recursor` feature flag. The `hickory-recursor` crate will not receive any updates going forward and all users should migrate to `hickory-resolver` with the `recursor` feature.

Users of the `hickory-dns` binary configured with the opt-in `recursor` feature and a configuration acting as a recursive resolver should update to 0.26.0+.

### Reporter 

Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-2hxp-x833-73f7.title: Hickory DNS recursor: ghost domain attack via child-side NS RRset queries
GHSA-2hxp-x833-73f7.description: **Reporter:** Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks The Hickory DNS recursor is susceptible to a 'ghost domain names' attack of CVE-2012-1033 / CVE-2022-30698. When a client sends `<zone>. IN NS` queries to the recursive resolver, the zone's apex NS RRset is retrieved from the zone's name servers, and stored in the response cache. This is later used when serving other queries from the same zone. The recursor may reuse this apex NS RRset when performing iterative resolution, so long as it is present in the cache. The NS RRset may be kept in the cache indefinitely with repeated queries. If the parent of the zone changes or removes its delegation, the recursor may continue performing iterative resolution using the old name servers, giving the old name servers control over responses past the revocation of their referral by the parent zone. The `hickory-recursor` crate is affected. Since 0.26.0-beta.1, the affected functionality has moved to the `hickory-resolver` crate, gated by the optional `recursor` feature.

An attacker who controls any secure zone in the public DNS can therefore produce a cryptographically-valid RRSIG over arbitrary records at an arbitrary name in an unrelated zone. The bug is reachable by any caller of `DnssecDnsHandle`, including the resolver, recursor, and client, when built with the `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs` feature and configured to perform DNSSEC validation. The affected code was migrated from `hickory-proto` to `hickory-net` as part of the 0.26.0 release, meaning `hickory-proto` versions 0.1 .. 0.25.0-alpha.3 are affected, while `hickory-proto` v0.25.0-alpha.4+ is not affected. Users of an affected configuration of `hickory-proto` versions 0.25.0-alpha.3 .. 0.25.2 are affected. GHSA-3r6v-f3jh-vvqm.title: ancestor-delegation NSEC accepted as proof of nonexistence below the zone cut
GHSA-3r6v-f3jh-vvqm.description: The validating recursor's NSEC handler does not distinguish parent-side delegation NSEC records from authoritative child-side NSECs. When a parent zone returns NXDOMAIN with the signed NSEC at the zone cut the implementation accepts that record as covering both the queried name and the synthesized wildcard, and returns `Proof::Secure`. The resolver then serves NXDOMAIN with AD=1 for names that legitimately exist in the child zone, contrary to RFC 6840 §4.1, which requires that an ancestor-delegation NSEC authenticate only the absence of DS at the cut owner and never the nonexistence of names below it. The forged response uses only records that are genuinely signed and publicly retrievable from the parent, so no key compromise is required; an attacker only needs to deliver one such response (on-path, via a rogue parent nameserver, or by winning a port+TXID race). Because the recursor caches the resulting negative under the (child., NS) key during its delegation walk, every subsequent client query for any name strictly below the cut short-circuits to the cached denial for up to the negative TTL. A similar issue affects validation of wildcard nonexistence proofs in NOERROR responses. There is another variant related to names with DNAME records, which are also mentioned in RFC 6840 §4.1. #### Reporter Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.title: Hickory DNS's Record Cache Accepts AUTHORITY-Section NS from Sibling Zone via Parent-Pool Zone-Context Elevation
GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.description:
# Summary

The Hickory DNS project's experimental `hickory-recursor` crate's record cache (`DnsLru`) stores records from DNS responses keyed by each record's own (name, type), not by the query that triggered the response. `cache_response()` in `crates/recursor/src/lib.rs` chains `ANSWER`, `AUTHORITY`, and `ADDITIONAL` sections into one record iterator before insertion. The bailiwick filter it applies uses the zone context of the NS pool that serviced the lookup, not the zone being queried.

This creates a cross-zone poisoning path. When Hickory builds the NS pool for `attacker.poc.` it uses the parent `poc.` `NS` pool (`ns.zone() = "poc."`). If the `poc.` nameserver under the attacker's control includes in its response's `AUTHORITY` section a record for a sibling zone like `victim.poc. NS ns.evil.poc.`, the bailiwick check `is_subzone("poc.", "victim.poc.")` passes (`victim.poc.` is a subdomain of `poc.`). The record is stored under `(victim.poc., NS)` in the shared cache.

Subsequently, any client querying a name in `victim.poc`. causes Hickory to build its NS pool from the poisoned cache entry, routing queries to the attacker's nameserver (`ns.evil.poc.`) rather than to the legitimate nameserver for `victim.poc.`. The legitimate `NS` for that zone receives zero queries.

This issue is fixed in `hickory-resolver` 0.26.0 with the `recursor` feature through an architectural change to response-level caching: responses are stored keyed by the originating query `(name, type)`. A response to `(attacker.poc. NS)` is stored only under that key and cannot affect the `(victim.poc., NS)` cache entry.

Hickory DNS believes this issue has been present in all published versions of the experimental `hickory-recursor` crate, which has now been folded into the `hickory-resolver` crate under the non-default `recursor` feature flag. The `hickory-recursor` crate will not receive any updates going forward and all users should migrate to `hickory-resolver` with the `recursor` feature.

Users of the `hickory-dns` binary configured with the opt-in `recursor` feature and a configuration acting as a recursive resolver should update to 0.26.0+.

### Reporter 

Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.title: Hickory DNS's Record Cache Accepts AUTHORITY-Section NS from Sibling Zone via Parent-Pool Zone-Context Elevation
GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.description:
# Summary

The Hickory DNS project's experimental `hickory-recursor` crate's record cache (`DnsLru`) stores records from DNS responses keyed by each record's own (name, type), not by the query that triggered the response. `cache_response()` in `crates/recursor/src/lib.rs` chains `ANSWER`, `AUTHORITY`, and `ADDITIONAL` sections into one record iterator before insertion. The bailiwick filter it applies uses the zone context of the NS pool that serviced the lookup, not the zone being queried.

This creates a cross-zone poisoning path. When Hickory builds the NS pool for `attacker.poc.` it uses the parent `poc.` `NS` pool (`ns.zone() = "poc."`). If the `poc.` nameserver under the attacker's control includes in its response's `AUTHORITY` section a record for a sibling zone like `victim.poc. NS ns.evil.poc.`, the bailiwick check `is_subzone("poc.", "victim.poc.")` passes (`victim.poc.` is a subdomain of `poc.`). The record is stored under `(victim.poc., NS)` in the shared cache.

Subsequently, any client querying a name in `victim.poc`. causes Hickory to build its NS pool from the poisoned cache entry, routing queries to the attacker's nameserver (`ns.evil.poc.`) rather than to the legitimate nameserver for `victim.poc.`. The legitimate `NS` for that zone receives zero queries.

This issue is fixed in `hickory-resolver` 0.26.0 with the `recursor` feature through an architectural change to response-level caching: responses are stored keyed by the originating query `(name, type)`. A response to `(attacker.poc. NS)` is stored only under that key and cannot affect the `(victim.poc., NS)` cache entry.

Hickory DNS believes this issue has been present in all published versions of the experimental `hickory-recursor` crate, which has now been folded into the `hickory-resolver` crate under the non-default `recursor` feature flag. The `hickory-recursor` crate will not receive any updates going forward and all users should migrate to `hickory-resolver` with the `recursor` feature.

Users of the `hickory-dns` binary configured with the opt-in `recursor` feature and a configuration acting as a recursive resolver should update to 0.26.0+.

### Reporter 

Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-2hxp-x833-73f7.title: Hickory DNS recursor: ghost domain attack via child-side NS RRset queries
GHSA-2hxp-x833-73f7.description: **Reporter:** Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks The Hickory DNS recursor is susceptible to a 'ghost domain names' attack of CVE-2012-1033 / CVE-2022-30698. When a client sends `<zone>. IN NS` queries to the recursive resolver, the zone's apex NS RRset is retrieved from the zone's name servers, and stored in the response cache. This is later used when serving other queries from the same zone. The recursor may reuse this apex NS RRset when performing iterative resolution, so long as it is present in the cache. The NS RRset may be kept in the cache indefinitely with repeated queries. If the parent of the zone changes or removes its delegation, the recursor may continue performing iterative resolution using the old name servers, giving the old name servers control over responses past the revocation of their referral by the parent zone. The `hickory-recursor` crate is affected. Since 0.26.0-beta.1, the affected functionality has moved to the `hickory-resolver` crate, gated by the optional `recursor` feature.

GHSA-2vgh-3wfw-qj7c.title: RRSIG Signer's Name not checked against the RRset's zone
GHSA-2vgh-3wfw-qj7c.description: Previously the Hickory DNS validator authenticated an RRset by fetching the DNSKEY RRset for whatever name appears in the RRSIG Signer's Name field and verifying the signature against that key, but never checked that the signer name is the zone that contains the RRset (as required by [RFC 4035 §5.3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4035#section-5.3.1), second bullet). An attacker who controls any secure zone in the public DNS can therefore produce a cryptographically-valid RRSIG over arbitrary records at an arbitrary name in an unrelated zone. The bug is reachable by any caller of `DnssecDnsHandle`, including the resolver, recursor, and client, when built with the `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs` feature and configured to perform DNSSEC validation. The affected code was migrated from `hickory-proto` to `hickory-net` as part of the 0.26.0 release, meaning `hickory-proto` versions 0.1 .. 0.25.0-alpha.3 are affected, while `hickory-proto` v0.25.0-alpha.4+ is not affected. Conversely all versions of `hickory-net` are affected until the patched version.

Users of an affected configuration of `hickory-proto` versions 0.25.0-alpha.3 .. 0.25.2 are affected. The affected code was migrated to the `hickory-net` crate, meaning affected configurations of `hickory-net` versions 0.26.0-alpha.1 .. 0.26.1 are affected. #### Reporter Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-3r6v-f3jh-vvqm.title: ancestor-delegation NSEC accepted as proof of nonexistence below the zone cut
GHSA-3r6v-f3jh-vvqm.description: The validating recursor's NSEC handler does not distinguish parent-side delegation NSEC records from authoritative child-side NSECs. When a parent zone returns NXDOMAIN with the signed NSEC at the zone cut the implementation accepts that record as covering both the queried name and the synthesized wildcard, and returns `Proof::Secure`. The resolver then serves NXDOMAIN with AD=1 for names that legitimately exist in the child zone, contrary to RFC 6840 §4.1, which requires that an ancestor-delegation NSEC authenticate only the absence of DS at the cut owner and never the nonexistence of names below it. The forged response uses only records that are genuinely signed and publicly retrievable from the parent, so no key compromise is required; an attacker only needs to deliver one such response (on-path, via a rogue parent nameserver, or by winning a port+TXID race). Because the recursor caches the resulting negative under the (child., NS) key during its delegation walk, every subsequent client query for any name strictly below the cut short-circuits to the cached denial for up to the negative TTL. A similar issue affects validation of wildcard nonexistence proofs in NOERROR responses. There is another variant related to names with DNAME records, which are also mentioned in RFC 6840 §4.1. #### Reporter Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.title: Hickory DNS's Record Cache Accepts AUTHORITY-Section NS from Sibling Zone via Parent-Pool Zone-Context Elevation
GHSA-83hf-93m4-rgwq.description:
# Summary

The Hickory DNS project's experimental `hickory-recursor` crate's record cache (`DnsLru`) stores records from DNS responses keyed by each record's own (name, type), not by the query that triggered the response. `cache_response()` in `crates/recursor/src/lib.rs` chains `ANSWER`, `AUTHORITY`, and `ADDITIONAL` sections into one record iterator before insertion. The bailiwick filter it applies uses the zone context of the NS pool that serviced the lookup, not the zone being queried.

This creates a cross-zone poisoning path. When Hickory builds the NS pool for `attacker.poc.` it uses the parent `poc.` `NS` pool (`ns.zone() = "poc."`). If the `poc.` nameserver under the attacker's control includes in its response's `AUTHORITY` section a record for a sibling zone like `victim.poc. NS ns.evil.poc.`, the bailiwick check `is_subzone("poc.", "victim.poc.")` passes (`victim.poc.` is a subdomain of `poc.`). The record is stored under `(victim.poc., NS)` in the shared cache.

Subsequently, any client querying a name in `victim.poc`. causes Hickory to build its NS pool from the poisoned cache entry, routing queries to the attacker's nameserver (`ns.evil.poc.`) rather than to the legitimate nameserver for `victim.poc.`. The legitimate `NS` for that zone receives zero queries.

This issue is fixed in `hickory-resolver` 0.26.0 with the `recursor` feature through an architectural change to response-level caching: responses are stored keyed by the originating query `(name, type)`. A response to `(attacker.poc. NS)` is stored only under that key and cannot affect the `(victim.poc., NS)` cache entry.

Hickory DNS believes this issue has been present in all published versions of the experimental `hickory-recursor` crate, which has now been folded into the `hickory-resolver` crate under the non-default `recursor` feature flag. The `hickory-recursor` crate will not receive any updates going forward and all users should migrate to `hickory-resolver` with the `recursor` feature.

Users of the `hickory-dns` binary configured with the opt-in `recursor` feature and a configuration acting as a recursive resolver should update to 0.26.0+.

### Reporter 

Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks

GHSA-929p-gjf6-5hqj.title: DNSSEC validation accepts responses with the wrong RRset as a positive answer
GHSA-929p-gjf6-5hqj.description: **Reporter:** Qifan Zhang, Palo Alto Networks The existing DNSSEC validation logic for positive responses only requires that there is some valid RRset in the answer section of the response, it does not check that the RRset is responsive to the query. If no records matching the query are present in a response, the response should be validated as if it were a 'no data' response instead.

GHSA-9px7-7m25-f6q2.title: Recursive resolver: Empty connection pool is cached after failed IP lookup
GHSA-9px7-7m25-f6q2.description: If the recursive resolver tries to follow a referral with no glue records, and all queries for IP addresses of name servers fail, a connection pool with no connections would be constructed and stored in a cache. All subsequent queries for the same zone would fail until the cache entry expires or is evicted. This issue could be triggered through a spoofing attack, and would cause a denial of service.

GHSA-p2jv-r3m3-7wf4.title: Nonexistence proof forgery due to insufficient checks on NSEC3 record names
GHSA-p2jv-r3m3-7wf4.description: DNSSEC verification performs insufficient checks on the names of NSEC3 records. The hash in the last label is compared against the hash of the query or record name being tested, but there is no check against the rest of the name to confirm that the NSEC3 record comes from the correct zone. As a result, this allows for forgery of nonexistence proofs.

GHSA-v44v-c8m4-gc43.title: Denial of service of client UDP connections via spoofed malformed responses
GHSA-v44v-c8m4-gc43.description: If a client UDP connection receives a datagram that cannot be parsed as a DNS message while it is listening for a response from a name server, it will stop listening and return an error. It is feasible for attackers to spoof messages that trigger this condition, causing a denial of service, because they only need to guess the port number used by the connection, and not the transaction ID of the client's query message. This is the DoS variant of the [TuDoor attack](https://lixiang521.com/publication/oakland24/sp24spring-tudoor-li.pdf).

GHSA-vrv5-968r-5ggm.title: DNSSEC validation accepts bogus positive response with wildcard expansion
GHSA-vrv5-968r-5ggm.description: DNSSEC validation does not sufficiently distinguish between NODATA respones and positive responses with wildcard expansion. If a query is made that should result in a NODATA response, and the zone has records with wildcard names, it is possible for an attacker to combine an NSEC3 record matching the query name, the record with a wildcard name, and its signature into a bogus positive response that will be accepted by DNSSEC validation. If the query name is proven to exist, then wildcard expansion should not be performed, and an answer section with a wildcard-expanded positive response should not be accepted.

GHSA-x962-5xwx-fr8x.description: When decoding a malformed TSIG record from the DNS wire format, it is possible to cause an arithmetic underflow. This results in a panic when compiling with the `dev` profile.
